title: Oaktree Capital — founded in 1995 as a distressed-debt specialist with Bruce Karsh
statement:
Marks, Bruce Karsh, Sheldon Stone, Larry Keele, and Stephen Kaplan left TCW Group in 1995 to found Oaktree Capital Management in Los Angeles, taking the high-yield and distressed-debt franchise with them after TCW refused to let them manage the funds in-house. The firm launched with a multi-billion-dollar AUM base transferred from TCW and an explicit focus on credit strategies that the rest of the industry had largely abandoned.

Oaktree's founding thesis was contrarian at the time: that the boring, illiquid, and out-of-favor corners of the credit markets offered persistently higher risk-adjusted returns than the glamorous equity strategies most investors chased. The firm's name — Oaktree, evoking slow growth and deep roots — captured the discipline the founders intended to apply to capital allocation.

The decision to focus on distressed rather than diversifying into the more profitable businesses of the era was unusual for an asset manager scaling in a bull market, but it set the conditions for Oaktree's later dominance of the distressed-debt category.
outcome:
Oaktree grew to manage over $100 billion within two decades and became, per Wikipedia and Crain's reporting, the largest investor in distressed securities worldwide. The decision to specialize rather than generalize produced an institutional franchise that competitors found difficult to replicate because the underwriting culture and the cycle-tested track record were built in the early, less-crowded years of the distressed category.

The firm's focus on credit cycles positioned it to deploy aggressively during the 2008 crisis, when Oaktree raised $10.9 billion for its Opportunities Fund VIIb and bought distressed assets at prices that, in Marks's words, 'paid off richly for his investors.' The founding choice of specialty over scale was vindicated by scale that followed specialty.

In 2012, Oaktree went public via IPO at $43 per share, raising $380 million; in 2019 Brookfield Asset Management acquired 62% of the firm while leaving Marks and Oaktree management in full control of day-to-day operations.

title: TCW's first distressed-debt fund — organized with Bruce Karsh in 1988
statement:
While at TCW Group, Marks and Bruce Karsh organized one of the first dedicated distressed-debt funds launched by a major financial institution. The fund was built to buy the debt of companies in or near bankruptcy at discounts that reflected panic rather than fundamental value.

The 1988 launch came on the heels of the leveraged buyout boom and the early signs of the savings-and-loan crisis, both of which were beginning to produce a wave of stressed and defaulted credits. The thesis was that the supply of distressed paper would outpace the number of investors equipped to evaluate it, and that the analytical work of understanding the bankruptcy process and the capital structure would be rewarded with returns unavailable to passive credit holders.

The fund represented an early institutional bet on distressed debt as an asset class rather than a one-off opportunity, and it formalized the underwriting discipline that would later become Oaktree's competitive moat.
outcome:
The fund became the seed of what grew into a multi-billion-dollar distressed franchise that, after the 1995 spin-out, became Oaktree's flagship strategy. Karsh went on to become Oaktree's co-founder and president, and the distressed-debt team became one of the most experienced in the industry, with cumulative deployed capital across cycles measured in the tens of billions.

The 1988 launch also coincided with the formation of the first distressed-debt indices and benchmarks, helping to legitimate the asset class for institutional investors who had previously viewed it as a niche speculative activity. The decision to institutionalize distressed investing has, in retrospect, been one of the more consequential capital-allocation decisions of the late-1980s credit markets.

The track record built at TCW between 1988 and 1995 is what attracted the institutional capital that allowed Oaktree to scale rapidly post-spin-out, and it set the underwriting template that Oaktree would later apply across the 1998 LTCM unwind, the 2000-2002 telecom defaults, the 2008-2009 financial crisis, and the 2020 COVID dislocations.

title: Opportunities Fund VIIb — raised $10.9B to deploy into the 2008-2009 credit collapse
statement:
In 2007 and 2008, as the subprime mortgage crisis began to spread through the credit markets, Oaktree raised approximately $10.9 billion for its Opportunities Fund VIIb — the largest distressed-debt fund ever raised at the time — explicitly to buy assets that the global financial system was being forced to liquidate. The fund closed and was deployed during the worst of the 2008-2009 panic, with capital committed to distressed corporate credit, structured products, and senior secured loans that had been marked down to prices implying default rates several times any historical level.

The decision to raise the fund in advance of the crisis — and to time its deployment to the panic rather than to the recovery — reflected Marks's view that the time to assemble distressed capital is before the distress arrives. By the time the dislocations were visible, the cost of raising fresh capital would have been prohibitive and the opportunity to commit at attractive prices would have passed.

Oaktree deployed the fund gradually through late 2008 and early 2009, buying into a market where the bid-ask spread had widened to a chasm and where the few investors with capital and conviction could name their price.
outcome:
The fund's investments, in Marks's public characterization, 'paid off richly for his investors.' The 2008-2009 deployment became the textbook example of how cycle-tested capital coupled with second-level thinking could capture returns unavailable to investors who lacked the dry powder to act during the panic.

The episode also reinforced Oaktree's positioning as the dominant distressed-debt franchise globally, and it set the conditions for the firm's subsequent growth as institutional investors increasingly sought credit specialists with proven crisis-deployment track records. Marks's 2008 memo 'Nobody Knows' framed the deployment philosophy that drove the fund — admission of uncertainty combined with action when prices compensate for that uncertainty.

Wikipedia and Oaktree's published materials both describe the $10.9 billion fund as the largest in the distressed category at the time of its raise, and the deployment is widely cited as one of the most consequential crisis-investing decisions of the post-2008 era.

title: Dot-com bubble — declined to participate meaningfully in technology equity mania
statement:
During the late-1990s technology and internet equity mania, Oaktree and Marks declined to participate meaningfully in the dot-com bubble. The firm stayed focused on its credit franchise — high-yield bonds, distressed debt, and convertible securities — rather than pivoting to the technology equities that the broader market was aggressively bidding up.

Marks wrote about the period in memos including 'Bubble.Com' (2000), 'We're Not In 1999 Anymore, Toto' (2000), and 'Irrational Exuberance' (2000), each of which identified the conditions of a bubble: valuations untethered from earnings, retail enthusiasm, and the assumption that a new paradigm had suspended the laws of economics. The decision to pass on the equity mania was consistent with Oaktree's circle of competence and with Marks's view that capital preservation is the precondition for participation in future dislocations.

The decision was uncomfortable at the time, as Oaktree's clients and competitors were underweight credit and overweight technology equity, and the relative underperformance during the bubble's peak created pressure to chase the same returns the rest of the market was capturing.
outcome:
When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000-2002, Oaktree's discipline was vindicated. The Nasdaq fell roughly 78% from its March 2000 peak to its October 2002 trough, while Oaktree's credit strategies — particularly distressed debt, which expanded as the technology unwind produced stressed credits across the telecom and cable sectors — generated opportunities that the equity mania had crowded out.

The decision to avoid the bubble preserved capital that was subsequently deployed into distressed opportunities the bubble's bursting created. Marks's later memos, including 'The Most Important Thing' (2003), drew on the dot-com episode as a case study in identifying the conditions of a bubble and in resisting the social and professional pressure to participate.

The avoidance of the dot-com bubble is one of the most cited decisions in Marks's public record and is widely referenced as the textbook example of the discipline that contrarian, second-level thinking requires during a mania.

title: LTCM collapse — avoided leveraged relative-value trades and bought the unwind
statement:
In 1998, when Long-Term Capital Management's highly leveraged relative-value trades collapsed and required a Federal Reserve-orchestrated bailout, Oaktree and Marks had avoided the strategies that LTCM had popularized — fixed-income arbitrage and leveraged convergence trades — on the grounds that the returns depended on leverage rather than on fundamental value and that the volatility was structural rather than episodic.

Marks's 1998 memo 'Genius Isn't Enough (And Other Lessons From Long Term Capital Management)' analyzed the failure as a case study in the limits of intelligence when intelligence is paired with leverage and overconfidence. The memo argued that the combination of high leverage, complexity, and the assumption that historical correlations would persist is the classic formula for catastrophic loss, regardless of the intellectual pedigree of the operators.

The decision to avoid LTCM-style strategies was consistent with Oaktree's broader discipline of avoiding leverage as a source of returns and of treating volatility as a feature of markets rather than a risk to be eliminated through structured products.
outcome:
LTCM's collapse in September 1998 required a $3.6 billion bailout organized by the New York Federal Reserve, and the episode became the canonical case study in the dangers of leverage plus intelligence plus overconfidence. Marks's memo on the episode became one of his most cited, and the lessons he drew — that intelligence is not a substitute for risk management, that leverage is the classic path to ruin, and that historical correlations can break precisely when leverage is highest — have been repeatedly re-cited in subsequent crises, including 2008 and 2020.

The avoidance of LTCM-style relative-value strategies preserved Oaktree's capital and positioned it to deploy into the credit dislocations that followed the LTCM unwind, when panicked selling of credit instruments created distressed opportunities unrelated to LTCM's specific trades.

The episode reinforced Marks's reputation as a credit investor who learns from the mistakes of others rather than repeating them, and it set the foundation for the underwriting discipline that drove Oaktree's subsequent deployment into the 2008 and 2020 crises.

title: Resolution Trust Corporation era — bought distressed assets from the S&L cleanup
statement:
During the early 1990s, in the wake of the savings-and-loan crisis and the formation of the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC) to dispose of the assets of failed thrifts, Marks and his team — first at TCW and then at Oaktree after the 1995 spin-out — bought distressed loans and real-estate assets from the RTC's portfolio at prices that reflected forced liquidation rather than fundamental value.

The RTC era was the first major post-war wave of institutional distressed-debt investing in the United States, and it produced the opportunity set that validated the underwriting discipline Marks and Karsh had begun to develop at TCW in 1988. The assets available included commercial real-estate loans, residential mortgages, and high-yield bonds of thrift-related issuers, all of which had been marked down to levels that implied widespread default and permanent loss.

The decision to deploy aggressively into RTC disposals — alongside other early distressed investors including Sam Zell and Wilbur Ross — was the foundation of Oaktree's first decade of returns and the proof of concept for the franchise Marks would later scale.
outcome:
Oaktree's investments during the RTC era produced returns that established the firm's track record and attracted the institutional capital that allowed it to grow into the dominant distressed franchise of the subsequent two decades. The RTC dispositions were eventually wound down by 1995-1996, but the underwriting discipline Oaktree developed during the period became the template for its deployment into the 1998 LTCM unwind, the 2000-2002 telecom defaults, the 2008-2009 financial crisis, and the 2020 COVID dislocations.

The RTC episode was historically significant because it marked the first time the U.S. government organized a systematic disposition program for distressed assets at scale, a model that would be partially reprised in 2008-2009 with the Public-Private Investment Program (PPIP). Marks has cited the RTC era in subsequent memos as the formative period in his education as a distressed investor and as the proof that distressed-debt investing, properly executed, produces risk-adjusted returns unavailable in any other credit strategy.

The S&L crisis and RTC cleanup are also the backdrop for Marks's early memos, including 'The Route to Performance' (1990), which laid out the philosophy of contrarian credit investing that the firm would apply for the next three decades.

title: COVID-19 dislocations — deployed into distressed debt during the March 2020 panic
statement:
In March 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the global economy and credit markets repriced at the fastest pace on record, Oaktree deployed capital into distressed debt and stressed credit dislocations. Marks published 'Nobody Knows II' on March 3, 2020, framing the decision in the same language he had used in the 2008 'Nobody Knows' memo — admission of macro uncertainty combined with action when prices compensate for that uncertainty.

The opportunity set in March 2020 was unusually compressed: high-yield bond spreads blew out to levels last seen in 2008-2009, senior secured loans traded at deep discounts to par, and structured credit was marked down mechanically as forced sellers liquidated leveraged positions. The dislocation was faster than 2008 — the S&P fell 33.9% in 32 days — but the recovery was also faster, with the index regaining its prior high in less than five months.

The decision to deploy aggressively during the panic required pre-positioned capital and a tolerance for being wrong in the short run. Oaktree's pre-existing dry powder and its mandate to invest counter-cyclically allowed the firm to act when most investors were forced to the sidelines.
outcome:
The COVID-19 deployment, like the 2008-2009 deployment, captured returns that were unavailable to investors who lacked the capital or the conviction to act during the panic. Marks's 'Nobody Knows II' memo and his subsequent 'Calibrating' (April 2020) memo laid out the framework that drove the deployment: scale in gradually as prices fall, trust the underlying mathematics of distressed credit, and resist the urge to wait for the all-clear signal that never comes at the bottom.

The episode reinforced Marks's three-time 'Nobody Knows' framework (2008, 2020, 2025) as the canonical statement of how a contrarian investor should respond to macro uncertainty. The decision to deploy rather than forecast the bottom distinguished Oaktree from investors who waited for clarity and missed the dislocation.

The COVID deployment also demonstrated that the cycle-tested discipline Oaktree built during the RTC era and refined through 1998, 2000-2002, and 2008-2009 was generalizable across crisis types — that the same underwriting muscles that worked during a financial-sector crisis worked during a pandemic-driven panic.

title: 'I don't know' macro stance — refused to forecast cycles, kept dry powder for dislocations
statement:
Throughout his career, and most explicitly in three memos titled 'Nobody Knows' (October 2008), 'Nobody Knows II' (March 2020), and 'Nobody Knows (Yet Again)' (April 2025), Marks has declined to forecast macro outcomes. The stance is not agnosticism — Marks has been clear about the conditions that produce bubbles, the pendulum swings of market psychology, and the structural risks in credit markets. The stance is the refusal to convert those observations into specific directional forecasts at moments when uncertainty is highest.

The 'I don't know' position is operationalized through three disciplines: raising capital for distress before the distress arrives, sizing positions so that the journey to vindication does not break the portfolio, and demanding a larger margin of safety when the range of outcomes has widened. The investor who admits uncertainty in real time is the investor who can act on dislocations when they appear.

The decision to hold this stance consistently — through the 2008 crisis, the 2020 pandemic, and the 2025 tariff shock — is itself a capital-allocation decision. The investor who refuses to forecast is the investor who retains optionality, and optionality is the asset that matters most when the unexpected arrives.
outcome:
The 'I don't know' stance has been vindicated across three crises. In each case, the investors who forecasted the bottom or the top were wrong often enough that their capital was mispositioned when the dislocation arrived. The investors who admitted uncertainty and retained dry powder were the investors who could act.

Oaktree's structural preparation — pre-raised distressed funds, a cycle-tested underwriting team, and a mandate to deploy counter-cyclically — was built specifically to operationalize the 'I don't know' stance. The firm has raised its distressed funds ahead of each major crisis (1988 ahead of the S&L cleanup, 2007-2008 ahead of the GFC, and ongoing dry powder ahead of the 2020 COVID dislocations), and the deployment during each crisis has produced returns unavailable to investors who waited for clarity.

The 'I don't know' framework is now widely cited as the canonical statement of how a credit investor should approach macro uncertainty, and it is one of the most influential ideas in the post-2008 institutional investing literature. The three Nobody Knows memos together form a body of work that defines the discipline Marks has applied for thirty-five years.

title: The 'third-level' memo on the tech bubble
statement: Marks wrote his memo 'bubble.com' explicitly applying second-level thinking — everyone knew tech companies would change the world, so the question was whether prices already discounted more than that — and refused the sector.
outcome: Oaktree's avoidance of technology equities through 2000-2002 preserved capital in the worst drawdown in a generation; the memo became the canonical statement of second-level thinking later elaborated in 'The Most Important Thing.'

title: Oaktree's European distressed expansion
statement: Marks and Karsh extended the distressed franchise to Europe, raising a European opportunities fund as the continent's banks began cycling nonperforming loans.
outcome: The expansion positioned Oaktree for the post-2008 European bank deleveraging, which became one of the firm's most profitable eras.

title: Raising the largest distressed fund ever after Lehman
statement: Six months after Lehman's fall, with prices at depression levels, Oaktree raised roughly $10.9 billion for Opportunities Fund VIIb — the largest distressed-debt fund ever raised.
outcome: The fund deployed into assets yielding double digits with equity-like returns, and Marks's memos from 2007-2009 ('The Race to the Bottom,' 'Nobody Knows,' 'The Limits to Negativism') became the era's definitive market chronicle.

title: Refusing to scale into illiquidity — the 2014 'lack of warning' stance
statement: As post-QE markets eliminated risk premiums, Marks systematically declined to extend duration or quality risk, writing that Oaktree would rather look wrong and safe than right and reckless.
outcome: The discipline cost some upside in the late 2010s rally but positioned the firm's funds for the 2020 dislocation; Marks's memos from the era taught an entire industry to treat the cycle, not the forecast, as the decision variable.
